title: List my orders (GET /orders?status=&sort=)
description: How a signed-in customer lists their own orders, filtered by status and sorted by a column, from the request to the SELECT ... ORDER BY statement flagged by Semgrep (src/repositories/orderRepository.js:8).

steps.title: Client: HTTP request
description: **What happens:** any user with an API token (role `user` or `admin`) asks for their orders. Both query parameters are optional: `status` filters, `sort` picks the ORDER BY column.
| No `Authorization` header, or not `Bearer …` | 401 | `{"error":"missing token"}` | captured |
| Token not in `users.api_token` | 401 | `{"error":"invalid token"}` | derived from code, not run |
| `status` not `open`/`shipped`/`cancelled` | 400 | `{"error":"invalid status"}` | derived from code, not run |
| `sort` is not a column Postgres accepts (e.g. `sort=price`) | 500 | `{"error":"internal error"}` | derived from code, not run |
| Success | 200 | JSON array of the caller's orders | derived from code, not run |
**Next →** Express matches the path against the mounted routers (step 2).

steps.title: App: mount orders router
description: **What happens:** the app installs the JSON and urlencoded body parsers, then mounts the orders router first. Query strings are parsed by Express 5's default `simple` parser (Node `querystring`): values are strings, a repeated key becomes an array.

steps.title: Routing: GET /orders
description: **What happens:** the route runs one middleware, `requireAuth`, then the controller. There is no `requireRole`, so every authenticated user reaches the controller.

steps.title: Auth: read Bearer token
description: **What happens:** takes the token from `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A missing header or any other scheme stops the request (captured from the running app):

steps.title: Auth: authenticate token
description: **What happens:** `userService.authenticate` forwards straight to `userRepository.findByToken`. No matching user stops the request; otherwise the user row is stored on `req.user`.

steps.title: Auth store: token lookup
steps.pattern: ('SELECT id, username, role FROM users WHERE api_token = \$1', \[token\])
description: **What happens:** looks the token up with a parameterised query: the token is sent as the value of `$1`, not as part of the SQL text.
req.user = { id: 1, username: 'alice', role: 'user' }   // for tok_alice_7d2f9c

steps.title: Controller: read status, sort
note: status, sort from the query string
description: **What happens:** both values come straight from the caller's query string.

steps.title: Controller: validate status
description: **What happens:** `status`, when present, must be one of `ALLOWED_STATUSES`. Anything else, including a repeated `status` key (an array), is rejected:
**Security:** there is no equivalent check for `sort`; it is passed on unchanged.

steps.title: Controller: rename sort
description: **What happens:** the query parameter `sort` becomes `filters.orderColumn`; the user id comes from `req.user`, not from the request.

steps.title: Service: default sort column
description: **What happens:** no business logic: when `sort` was omitted, the column defaults to `created_at`. The value is the third argument, named `orderBy` in the repository.

steps.title: Store: ORDER BY interpolation
description: **What happens:** `orderBy` is written into the SQL text with a template literal. This is the line Semgrep flagged (`orderRepository.js:8`, statement starts there).
SELECT id, total, status, created_at FROM orders
WHERE user_id = $1 AND ($2::text IS NULL OR status = $2)
**Security:** the text after `ORDER BY` is whatever `sort` contained; a repeated `sort` key becomes an array and is joined with commas (`?sort=a&sort=b` → `ORDER BY a,b`).
**Next →** the parameter values sent with it (step 12).

steps.title: Store: bound parameters
description: **What happens:** `userId` and `status` are sent as bound parameters `$1` and `$2`. Only `orderBy` is part of the SQL text.

steps.title: Postgres: run the SELECT
description: **What happens:** Postgres parses the statement (including the `ORDER BY` text) and runs it with the bound values. An unknown column name is a parse error, e.g. `column "price" does not exist`, which rejects the `pool.query` promise.
**Next →** rows back to the controller (step 14) or the error handler (step 15).
